idiom_name: typed arrow closure (optionally with a curry-typed helper)
implementation_notes: The runtime answer is the same as JavaScript's - an arrow closure that binds the leading arguments and declares the remaining arity, `const add5: (y: number) => number = (y) => add(5, y);` - and the type system adds the part that matters, because the specialised function's signature is written down and checked at every call site. bind is usable for reusable code only when strictBindCallApply is enabled; TypeScript 3.2's notes document the option and its caveat that generic functions and overloads are not modelled. Optional and default parameters remain the idiomatic substitute when the specialisation is a call-site concern; library-wide currying (Ramda-style) needs the curried types declared explicitly, since inference does not derive them.
pitfalls: bind, call and apply do not model generic functions or overloads: type parameters are substituted with {} and only the last overload is considered (documented caveat of strictBindCallApply), so a bound generic silently loses type safety - write an explicit wrapper arrow instead.

Optional parameters survive specialisation as T | undefined, so a bound function can still demand an argument the caller believed was fixed; make the bound parameters required in the arrow's own signature.

Arrow closures have no this: binding a method with .bind keeps the runtime receiver, but typing it needs ThisParameterType/OmitThisParameter, and extracting a this-dependent method into a bare function compiles fine and fails at runtime.
